blurb: How AI paints pictures out of static, how words steer it, how video works — and how to tell what's real.

steps.p: Take millions of real photos and add random speckles (noise) to them, a little at a time, until each one is pure TV static.

steps.h: Step 2: learn to undo one step
steps.p: Train a network to look at a noisy image and predict the noise that was added — so it can be subtracted, making the image slightly cleaner.
steps.analogy: Like restoring an old, scratched photo one tiny scratch at a time.

steps.p: To make a new image, start with random static and run the clean-up step again and again — often dozens of times. A brand-new picture gradually appears.
To remove noise well, the network must learn what real images look like — fur, faces, light. Run in reverse, that knowledge creates images.
From 2014, GANs led the field: a forger network makes fakes and a detective network tries to spot them. Both improve — but training was unstable.

cards.q: During training, a diffusion model's network usually learns to predict…
options: The noise that was added to a noisy image
cards.why: The added noise. If you can predict the noise, you can subtract it. Doing that step after step turns static into a picture.

cards.statement: Diffusion models traditionally produce an image in a single pass.
cards.why: False. They clean up the image over many steps — often 20 to 50. Newer tricks cut this down, which is why generation keeps getting faster.

cards.q: Before diffusion, GANs led image generation. A GAN trains…
options: A forger network against a detective network that tries to spot its fakes
Two copies of the same photo
cards.why: Forger vs detective. The generator improves until the discriminator can't tell real from fake. It produced sharp images, but training could easily go wrong.

cards.title: Ian Goodfellow reportedly came up with GANs in 2014 after a debate with friends at a Montreal bar.
cards.detail: By his own account he went home, coded it that night, and it worked on the first try.

cards.statement: GANs are known for unstable training and "mode collapse", where they produce only a few kinds of output.
cards.why: True. The forger can find a few fakes that fool the detective and stop exploring. Diffusion models are steadier and cover more variety.

cards.title: How Stable Diffusion turns words into pictures

steps.p: Working on millions of pixels is slow. So an encoder first squeezes the image into a small "latent" — a compact summary, maybe 48 times smaller.
steps.analogy: Planning a painting as a small sketch before working on the full canvas.

steps.p: All the noise-removing happens on that small summary, which is far cheaper. A decoder then expands it back into a full image with fine detail.
Your prompt is turned into embeddings, and at every clean-up step the network is nudged toward an image matching them.
Guidance compares "what it would draw with your prompt" and "without it", then exaggerates the difference. More guidance follows the prompt more closely but with less variety.
You can also say what you don't want ("blurry, extra fingers"), and guidance steers away from it.

cards.q: Why does Stable Diffusion work on a shrunk version instead of directly on pixels?
options: It's far cheaper, and a decoder restores the fine detail
cards.hint: Sketch first, then the full canvas.
cards.why: Speed. Cleaning a small summary dozens of times is much cheaper than cleaning millions of pixels, which is what made it run on ordinary graphics cards.

cards.q: Turning up the guidance scale usually makes images…
options: Follow the prompt more closely but with less variety
cards.why: Closer to the prompt, less varied. Too much can make images look over-saturated or harsh, so a middle setting is usual.

cards.statement: Stable Diffusion's trained model was released publicly for anyone to download.
cards.why: True. Its 2022 open release let anyone run it on a home computer, which sparked a huge wave of tools and add-ons.

cards.title: Stable Diffusion was trained using LAION-5B: about 5.85 billion image–caption pairs collected from the web.
cards.detail: Its size gave the model broad visual knowledge, but it also contained copyrighted and problematic images — leading to lawsuits and later clean-ups.

options: Steering away from what the negative prompt describes during each step
cards.why: Steering away. Guidance normally pushes away from the "no prompt" version; a negative prompt replaces that with things you specifically want to avoid.

steps.h: A video is a stack of images
steps.p: About 24 images per second. Generating each separately gives flicker — a cat's spots would change every frame.
Video models cut footage into small blocks spanning space and time, and a transformer attends across all of them — so frame 50 can "see" frame 1.
steps.analogy: Like cutting a flip-book into little cubes, each holding a patch of several pages.

steps.p: Diffusion Transformers (DiT) replaced the older U-Net design inside the denoiser and scale up better with more computing.
Keeping a face, an object count and physics believable across hundreds of frames is far harder than one good picture.
Newer methods like flow matching learn straighter routes from static to image, so fewer steps are needed.

cards.q: Diffusion Transformers (DiT) replaced which part of earlier diffusion models?
cards.why: The denoiser. Swapping the U-Net for a transformer let image and video models grow bigger and better in the predictable way language models do.

cards.statement: Keeping things consistent across frames is a main reason video is harder to generate than images.
cards.why: True. A single image just has to look right. A video must keep the same character, lighting and believable motion for every frame.

cards.q: Flow matching, used in newer models, learns…
options: Straighter paths from noise to image, so fewer steps are needed
cards.why: Straighter paths. A curvy route needs many small steps to follow; a straight one can be covered in a few big ones.

cards.title: OpenAI's Sora preview in February 2024 showed videos up to a minute long, made from text.
cards.detail: Earlier text-to-video models produced a few seconds of often wobbly footage. Sora's length and coherence reset expectations across the field.

cards.statement: Images can also be generated token by token, the way chatbots write text.
cards.why: True. Some models split images into tokens and predict them one after another. Several of today's chat assistants generate images this way.

cards.title: Proving where a picture came from

steps.p: AI images and video are now often hard to tell from real ones by eye. Three approaches try to help.
The generator hides an invisible signal in the pixels that software can later detect. Google's SynthID does this.
steps.analogy: Like the invisible security thread in a banknote.

steps.p: Cameras and editing apps can attach a tamper-evident record: who made this, with what, and every edit since — like a passport for the image.
Programs guess whether an image is AI-made. They can be useful hints but give false alarms and are easy to fool.
The most reliable step is still old-fashioned: where did this come from, and does a trustworthy source confirm it?

options: A signed record of how a piece of media was created and edited
cards.why: A signed history. If the record is intact and valid, you can see where an image came from. If it's missing, that proves nothing either way.

cards.statement: Today's AI-image detectors are reliable enough to prove an image is fake.
cards.why: False. They make mistakes both ways and can be fooled by simple edits. Treat them as a hint, not proof.

cards.q: Why is attached metadata alone a weak defence?
options: Screenshots and re-uploads often strip it
cards.hint: What happens when someone screenshots an image?
cards.why: It's easily lost. A screenshot is a brand-new image with no history attached. Signed records prove origin when present, but absence means little.

cards.title: Google's SynthID hides an invisible watermark in AI-generated images — and in text too.
cards.detail: For text, it subtly nudges word choices in a pattern software can detect. Google open-sourced the text version in 2024.

cards.title: Verify before you share
cards.body: Shocking image or clip? Pause. Look for the original source, and check whether trusted news outlets are reporting it.
cards.challenge: Next time a dramatic image goes viral in your feeds, try a reverse image search before believing or sharing it.
